projects.title: Neon Rush
projects.tagline: A three-lane endless runner for the browser, built small but structured like a production game.
summary: Neon Rush is my take on the endless runner: three lanes, a jump, a slide, three kinds of hazard, pickups with a combo multiplier, and a difficulty curve that speeds the run up without shrinking the time you have to react.

It is a small game on purpose. I used it to show how I set up a Unity project that is expected to grow: modules with enforced boundaries, rules that run without the engine, content as data, and one codebase for the browser, Windows and Android. It is still in development, and the browser build is the one being worked on.
highlights: The title screen is a camera shot. Press play and the camera swings round behind the runner as the run begins.
Keyboard, gamepad, mouse and touch, with on-screen hints that follow the devices in use.
Every screen works from keys or a gamepad, and the run pauses when the window loses focus.
A crash you can see: a flash, a camera shake, sparks, and a game-over screen that waits for it to play out.
Sound effects and two music loops that crossfade between the title and the run. The audio is placeholder for now.
Seeded runs and a saved best score.
architecture: Four layers, each its own assembly: App, Features, Shared and Core. A feature cannot reference another feature. They talk through messages and small interfaces, which is how sound, effects and the cameras were added without touching gameplay code.

Game rules and UI presenters are plain C# with no MonoBehaviour, so they are covered by EditMode tests, including tests that fail if a frame of gameplay allocates. One simulation loop ticks every system in a fixed order. What differs between platforms is data: an input profile and settings per platform family, with no platform checks in gameplay or UI code.
learned: Measure on the real thing. The score display built no strings and passed its allocation test, and still allocated about 360 bytes on every change once it was on screen, because UI Toolkit allocates whenever a label's text changes. It is now a row of reels that slide, and a test measures whole frames on the live HUD.
The numbers above come from a fast desktop and a local server. They show what the game costs, not how it runs on a slow laptop or a phone, which I have not measured yet.

projects.title: Cine Director
projects.tagline: First Light: a 78-second film shot with Cinemachine and cut on one Timeline, with notes on every shot.
projects.role: Solo: direction, code, set, sound, build
summary: First Light is a short film made entirely inside Unity. A maintenance robot wakes in a dead station, walks a corridor on emergency lighting, throws the lever that brings the power back, crosses a bridge in the open air and watches a beacon light as the sun comes up.

I made it to show camera work and sequencing the way I would do them in a shipped game: not a baked video, but data on a timeline, played by a small app you can pause, skip through by chapter and read. A bar above the picture names each shot, the technique behind it and the lens, as the camera goes live.
highlights: Twelve shots, twelve techniques: a dolly on a spline, a rack focus, a tracking shot, hand-held, over the shoulder, an insert, a cut on a signal, a static frame, an orbit, a crane, a dolly zoom and a pull-back.
Director's notes in the top bar, which you can switch off with N.
Five chapters. Skip between them or jump to any one from the pause panel; picture, lighting and sound are right on the next frame, forwards or backwards.
A robot that walks without a single animation clip: the gait is driven by distance travelled and the legs are solved with IK.
A score that follows the chapters and ten effects, all synthesised for the film and kept in step with the picture.
Keyboard, mouse or gamepad. Leaving the tab pauses the film.
architecture: One rule shaped the project: everything you see or hear is worked out from the film's current time, and nothing remembers the frame before. The walker, the lamps, the doors, the dawn, the cameras and the sound are each a small custom Timeline track over a component that applies what it is given. That is why a jump to any chapter needs no reset code.

Around the film is the same structure as my other projects: App, Features, Shared and a core package, each its own assembly, wired by dependency injection. The transport, the screens and the camera notes are plain C# classes covered by EditMode tests, and eight PlayMode tests run the whole app from its first scene.
learned: Look at the picture where it will be watched. My editor screenshots were rendered into an 8-bit target, which clamps the image before bloom runs, so bloom looked absent and I kept turning it up. The first browser build showed the real thing: a halo round every lamp.

A set made of 249 boxes cost 1,226 draw calls on the title card alone. Merging everything that never moves brought that to 461, in pieces kept small enough that each one is still lit by the lamps nearest to it.
The numbers above come from a fast desktop and a local server. They show what the film costs, not how it runs on a slow laptop or a phone, which I have not measured yet.

projects.title: Tactica AI
projects.tagline: Grid tactics against a hand-written behaviour tree that shows its reasoning for every move.
projects.role: Solo: design, code, AI, models, sound, build
summary: A small turn-based tactics game: three units a side on a six by six board with walls and cover. You can play Blue against the AI, or let it play both sides and watch.

The point of it is the panel on the right. Game AI is easy to fake, so I built an opponent you can check: every time one of its units decides, the panel lays out the whole decision. Each node of its behaviour tree with yes, no or never asked and the reason, then the options it weighed with the score written out term by term. It is the record the tree writes while it runs, not a description made up afterwards.
highlights: A behaviour tree I wrote by hand, with scoring at its leaves: the tree picks what kind of thing to do (finish a kill, fall back, strike, close in) and a weighted sum over the facts picks exactly where and to whom.
Three unit classes with three different trees: a brawler, a skirmisher that shoots from the safest spot it can find, and a medic that heals whoever is worst off.
A decision inspector with history. Step back through every decision of the match while it carries on.
A danger map you can switch on: how much the enemy could do to each cell next turn. It is the AI's own map, worked out for the unit about to move.
No dice anywhere. The same position always gives the same decision, and a match between the two AIs plays out move for move the same in the editor and in the browser.
Keyboard or mouse, with a layout for wide screens and one for a screen held upright.
architecture: The rules are a library with no engine in it: board, movement, line of fire, combat and turns, as plain C# that tests can play without starting Unity. There is one way to change a battle, which is to hand it an action and have the rules check it. A click and an AI decision go through the same call, so the AI cannot do anything a player could not.

Trees, unit classes and arenas are assets. A tree is a ScriptableObject with its nodes inside it; a new kind of unit is an asset with numbers, a model and a tree; an arena is six strings. Around that is the same structure as my other projects: App, Features, Shared and a core package, each its own assembly, wired by dependency injection.

What you see lags what is true, on purpose. The rules settle an action at once and the board plays it out from a queue, one step at a time. The AI waits for the board before its next step, which is why you can watch it think one unit at a time.
learned: Tests that put each shipped tree into a position drawn for one behaviour found a real flaw in the AI. A unit judged how dangerous a cell was with itself still standing where it was, so in a corridor it fell back one cell to a spot the enemy could still reach. With that fixed, a match between the two AIs went from five turns to ten.

The first browser build made about 400 draw calls for six units. Every model was ten primitives, each drawn for colour, again for ambient occlusion and again for four shadow cascades. Merging each model into one mesh per material and cutting the render pipeline down to what a small board needs brought a match to between 85 and 137.

The first match began with a frame of nearly a second, because everything was drawn for the first time on the frame after Play was pressed. The board now draws itself once while the app starts, behind a cover, and the first match's longest frame is 12.5 ms.
The numbers above come from a fast desktop and a local server. They show what the game costs, not how it runs on a slow laptop or a phone, which I have not measured yet.
